fetched_contents.text: State of Design: Only the Innovative Will Survive Editor’s Note: This story first appeared in the print edition of the 2026 State of the Majors. Click here to see the full issue. The jewelry industry has been struggling under the weight of the unprecedented price of gold but among jewelry designers, a trait is emerging from the tumult. The best among them are not just making thinner pieces or repricing merchandise over and over again. They are learning to be more flexible, creative, and intentional. Designers are embracing the use of materials like wood and leather, creating smaller yet more thoughtful collections, and in some cases, leaning into the investment value of gold when telling stories through their jewelry. To paraphrase one designer interviewed for this story, the only way out is to follow the gold price, which has gone straight up. In 2025, gold was $2,625 an ounce. So far in 2026, the price has basically doubled ($5,340 was its 2026 peak as of press time), says David Siminski, vice president of sales and marketing at United Precious Metals. The problem is not just gold. The other precious metals have followed its path. Platinum was $800 an ounce in 2025. As of press time, it was about $1,960. Silver has gone up almost 300 percent, from $28 an ounce in 2025 to a peak of $114 so far in 2026, and Siminski thinks it could hit $500. “That has created unbelievable chaos for many people. [With] the tariffs, it’s almost like the perfect storm,” he says. There are numerous contributing factors, one of the biggest being a lack of confidence in the U.S. dollar and U.S. Treasury-backed derivatives, according to Siminski. “With all the fallout when it comes to the current presidency and the constant bickering back and forth with geopolitical stuff, a lot of countries and central banks are buying physical metal. They’re driving up the price,” he explains. He notes that the other factor is retail investors “hitching onto the wagon” by adding or increasing the amount of metal in their portfolios through physical metal purchases, exchange-traded funds, or stocks. “Gold is like another form of currency because there’s a real question about the U.S. dollar, which has been the stabilizing factor around the world,” Siminski says. Metal is also in demand in the electronics industry, specifically gold and copper, for the circuit boards found in computers, phones, and cars. That drives up the price too. > “The rising price of gold has certainly changed the conversation, but it hasn’t diluted the creativity. If anything, it’s pushed designers to be even more intentional.” –Jennifer Shanker, Muse Siminski predicts that, based on gold’s trajectory, it will continue to rise for years and could reach $10,000 an ounce. He believes that one day people will look back at $5,000 gold as a bargain. “Even if gold or silver corrects by 10 percent or even 20 percent, it doesn’t matter,” he says. “Usually what happens is, it’ll fall, it’ll build a base, it’ll go up a little higher, then come back down. This is just shooting up like a rocket ship.” The Trend Rising with the Price of Gold One trend coming to the forefront as the price of gold continues to increase is the use of alternative materials. Major high-end brand collections and their 2021-2023 design themes
The evidence points to a strong emphasis on thematic and symbolic storytelling in high-end jewelry, with brands drawing on nature, heritage, and poetic inspiration. Van Cleef & Arpels’ high-jewelry collections are described as timeless, feminine, and designed to enhance the natural beauty of stones and the brilliance of metals, with thematic collections inspired by nature, couture, dance, literature, and love stories [N1-F1]. The same source also notes Heritage collections paying homage to the Maison’s legacy, from Art Deco to the 1980s [N1-F1]. This indicates continuity with historical motifs while allowing new thematic interpretations.

Chaumet’s 2026 high-jewelry collection is explicitly inspired by “the flavors of the natural world,” including evocations of tea fields, coffee aroma, and verbena [N4-R1]. This suggests a move toward nature-inspired abstraction and sensory symbolism, blending the organic with the poetic. The evidence also highlights broader jewelry trends toward botanical motifs, where flowers and nature become wearable art and carry symbolic meanings such as love, devotion, purity, and rebirth [N4-R2]. Art Deco-era motifs are similarly referenced as bold, geometric, and modernist, with zigzag patterns and sunburst motifs reflecting jazz rhythms and the dawn of modernity [N4-R3]. These motifs indicate that high-end brands are not abandoning traditional aesthetic language but reinterpreting it through contemporary cultural and artistic lenses.

How craftsmanship and materials evolved or remained traditional
Craftsmanship evidence suggests a mix of tradition and innovation. Van Cleef & Arpels’ brand messaging emphasizes classic high jewelry, with a focus on platinum, stones, and timeless feminine forms [N1-F1]. This implies that traditional craftsmanship remains central to the brand’s identity. At the same time, the broader jewelry industry is described as experimenting with alternative materials such as wood, leather, glass, and papier mache, not just for cost savings but as a creative and intentional design strategy [N3-F3]. This signals a shift toward material experimentation, especially as precious-metal prices rose sharply in 2025–2026, driving designers to be “more flexible, creative, and intentional” [N3-F3].

The evidence also points to sustainability-driven material choices. Prada’s 2022 Eternal Gold collection used 100% recycled gold and lab-grown diamonds (LGDs), while LVMH’s TAG Heuer integrated LGDs into timepieces [N3-R2]. Brilliant Earth and Alara emphasize recycled precious metals, reduced carbon footprint, and traceability, with claims that recycled gold is chemically identical to newly mined gold and causes “drastically reduced landscape disruption” [N3-R4][N6-R1]. This shows that craftsmanship is being redefined through ethical sourcing and circular production, even as traditional techniques remain important.

Notable limited editions, collaborations, and celebrity-driven launches
The evidence does not provide a comprehensive catalog of limited editions or collaborations across 2021–2023, so this section is more suggestive than definitive. However, it does show that brand identity is increasingly tied to exclusivity and signature collections. Van Cleef & Arpels’ Heritage and Signature collections are described as icons of the Maison’s know-how and timeless expressions of its enchanted vision [N1-F1]. This implies that limited-edition or heritage-inspired pieces are a deliberate part of brand storytelling.

The broader jewelry industry evidence suggests that designers are leaning into the investment value of gold and creating smaller, more thoughtful collections [N3-F3]. Muse, which represents several fine-jewelry brands, is noted as emphasizing meaningful rather than excessive pieces and one-of-a-kinds [N3-F3]. This points to a trend in limited or bespoke launches that appeal to both exclusivity and personal significance.

The evidence also hints at celebrity influence and experiential branding. The 2023 Sotheby’s auction report mentions Hollywood icons and rare jewels associated with them [N2-F2], while the luxury market report notes that social media influencers and celebrities influence consumer choices through high-impact campaigns on platforms such as Instagram, YouTube, etc. [N5-R3]. While this is not a direct brand collaboration, it shows that celebrity-driven narratives and experiential marketing are shaping high-end jewelry’s public image and consumer perception.

Overall, the 2021–2023 period appears to be one in which high-end jewelry brands are preserving their heritage and craftsmanship while experimenting with new materials, themes, and exclusivity strategies. Nature-inspired motifs, heritage collections, and sustainability-driven sourcing are central, while limited editions and experiential narratives are helping to maintain brand relevance and consumer engagement [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N3-F3][N3-R2][N5-R3].

The auction evidence is strongest on 2023, with Sotheby’s Magnificent Jewels auction totaling $95.9 million and featuring several record-breaking items. The auction included the Estrela de FURA: 55.22, a 55.22-carat Mozambique ruby that sold for $34.8 million and set a new auction record for a ruby and any colored gemstone [N2-F2]. The Eternal Pink, a 10.57-carat Fancy Vivid Purplish Pink diamond, also sold for $34.8 million, setting a world auction record for that color grade and a new price-per-carat record [N2-F2]. The auction also included a 33.51-carat Burmese sapphire ring by Cartier that sold for $3.3 million [N2-F2].

Sotheby’s Geneva auction included the Bulgari Laguna Blu, a 11.16-carat Fancy Vivid Blue diamond that mounted by Bulgari sold for CHF22,625,100 ($25,189,429) [N2-F2]. The report emphasizes that the diamond became the largest blue diamond ever to grace a Bulgari jewel and the most valuable gemstone mounted by Bulgari sold at auction [N2-F2]. Another notable item was the 133.03-carat Fancy Vivid Yellow diamond, the largest diamond of the color grade ever to sell at auction, which brought $5.5 million [N2-F2]. The report also highlights a 17.55-carat Burmese pink sapphire and diamond ring that sold for $1.1 million, over seven times its high estimate [N2-F2].

In addition to diamonds and gemstones, the auction evidence includes vintage and historically significant jewels. The Vienna 1900: An Imperial and Royal Collection returned to Geneva and achieved a “white glove” result with 100% of lots sold [N2-F2]. This indicates that high-value competition items are not limited to new gems but also include rare, provenanced vintage pieces with strong cultural and historical appeal [N2-F2].

How haute couture jewelry differs from standard luxury jewelry
The evidence distinguishes haute couture jewelry from standard luxury jewelry by its scale, exclusivity, and thematic ambition. Haute Couture Week in Paris is described as a platform for high-jewelry collections from major haute couture houses, with reports on the collections from that event [N2-R1]. The 2023 auction report also notes that the most valuable pieces often come from legendary maisons and include rare, one-off gems and vintage jewels [N2-F2]. This suggests that haute couture jewelry is typically associated with the most extreme levels of craftsmanship, rarity, and brand legacy.

A key difference is that haute couture jewelry often functions as both an artistic object and a cultural artifact. The 2023 Sotheby’s report highlights pieces with compelling provenance, such as the Vienna 1900 collection hidden in a bank vault for over seventy-five years and bound together by beauty, rarity, and illustrious provenances [N2-F2]. This contrasts with standard luxury jewelry, which is often more focused on contemporary design and commercial appeal. The report also notes that auction houses highlight not only the physical gemstones but also the stories behind them, including their provenance, rarity, and the cultural or historical context in which they were created [N2-F2].

Market dynamics and buyer behavior for high-value competition pieces
The market dynamics described in the evidence indicate that high-value competition pieces are driven by rarity, provenance, and the symbolic value of the gem or piece. The 2023 auction results show record prices for extremely rare colored gemstones, including the Estrela de FURA: 55.22 ruby and the Eternal Pink diamond [N2-F2]. These items attracted intense bidding, with some pieces selling after prolonged battles among multiple bidders [N2-F2]. The report also notes that rare, one-off gems and iconic vintage jewels are particularly sought after by connoisseurs, suggesting that buyers are willing to pay premium prices for exclusivity and heritage [N2-F2].

Buyer behavior appears to be shaped by both investment logic and emotional value. The luxury market report states that consumers increasingly value customized and heritage-inspired designs, ethically sourced gemstones, and transparent supply chains [N5-F4]. While this is more general, it supports the idea that buyers of high-value jewelry are looking for more than just aesthetics; they also care about authenticity, rarity, and the narrative attached to the item [N5-F4]. The auction evidence also suggests that provenance and historical significance can dramatically increase a piece’s market value, as seen in the Vienna 1900 collection and the Bulgari Laguna Blu [N2-F2].

In terms of market structure, the evidence points to strong demand for rare, one-off gems and for iconic vintage jewels that represent the best the great houses had to offer [N2-F2]. At the same time, the luxury market report notes that high product prices remain a key restraint, limiting accessibility beyond affluent consumer segments, and that economic uncertainty and inflationary pressures can delay discretionary purchases [N5-F4]. This means that high-value competition pieces are likely to be bought by high-net-worth individuals and collectors, rather than by broader mass markets [N5-F4].

Overall, haute couture jewelry and auction/high-value competition items stand out for their rarity, provenance, and symbolic weight. They differ from standard luxury jewelry in their scale of ambition, the depth of cultural or historical narrative, and the way they are marketed and valued by collectors and connoisseurs [N2-R1][N2-F2][N5-F4].

Major high-end brand collections and their 2021-2023 design themes
The evidence points to a strong emphasis on thematic and symbolic storytelling in high-end jewelry, with brands drawing on nature, heritage, and poetic inspiration. Van Cleef & Arpels’ high-jewelry collections are described as timeless, feminine, and designed to enhance the natural beauty of stones and the brilliance of metals, with thematic collections inspired by nature, couture, dance, literature, and love stories [N1-F1]. The same source also notes Heritage collections paying homage to the Maison’s legacy, from Art Deco to the 1980s [N1-F1]. This indicates continuity with historical motifs while allowing new thematic interpretations.

Chaumet’s 2026 high-jewelry collection is explicitly inspired by “the flavors of the natural world,” including evocations of tea fields, coffee aroma, and verbena [N4-R1]. This suggests a move toward nature-inspired abstraction and sensory symbolism, blending the organic with the poetic. The evidence also highlights broader jewelry trends toward botanical motifs, where flowers and nature become wearable art and carry symbolic meanings such as love, devotion, purity, and rebirth [N4-R2]. Art Deco-era motifs are similarly referenced as bold, geometric, and modernist, with zigzag patterns and sunburst motifs reflecting jazz rhythms and the dawn of modernity [N4-R3]. These motifs indicate that high-end brands are not abandoning traditional aesthetic language but reinterpreting it through contemporary cultural and artistic lenses.

How craftsmanship and materials evolved or remained traditional
Craftsmanship evidence suggests a mix of tradition and innovation. Van Cleef & Arpels’ brand messaging emphasizes classic high jewelry, with a focus on platinum, stones, and timeless feminine forms [N1-F1]. This implies that traditional craftsmanship remains central to the brand’s identity. At the same time, the broader jewelry industry is described as experimenting with alternative materials such as wood, leather, glass, and papier mache, not just for cost savings but as a creative and intentional design strategy [N3-F3]. This signals a shift toward material experimentation, especially as precious-metal prices rose sharply in 2025–2026, driving designers to be “more flexible, creative, and intentional” [N3-F3].

The evidence also points to sustainability-driven material choices. Prada’s 2022 Eternal Gold collection used 100% recycled gold and lab-grown diamonds (LGDs), while LVMH’s TAG Heuer integrated LGDs into timepieces [N3-R2]. Brilliant Earth and Alara emphasize recycled precious metals, reduced carbon footprint, and traceability, with claims that recycled gold is chemically identical to newly mined gold and causes “drastically reduced landscape disruption” [N3-R4][N6-R1]. This shows that craftsmanship is being redefined through ethical sourcing and circular production, even as traditional techniques remain important.

However, it does show that brand identity is increasingly tied to exclusivity and signature collections. While this is not a direct brand collaboration, it shows that celebrity-driven narratives and experiential marketing are shaping high-end jewelry’s public image and consumer perception.

Overall, the 2021–2023 period appears to be one in which high-end jewelry brands are preserving their heritage and craftsmanship while experimenting with new materials, themes, and exclusivity strategies. Nature-inspired motifs, heritage collections, and sustainability-driven sourcing are central, while limited editions and experiential narratives are helping to maintain brand relevance and consumer engagement [N1-F1][N4-R1][N4-R2][N3-F3][N3-R2][N5-R3].

The report emphasizes that the diamond became the largest blue diamond ever to grace a Bulgari jewel and the most valuable gemstone mounted by Bulgari sold at auction [N2-F2]. Another notable item was the 133.03-carat Fancy Vivid Yellow diamond, the largest diamond of the color grade ever to sell at auction, which brought $5.5 million [N2-F2]. The evidence distinguishes haute couture jewelry from standard luxury jewelry by its scale, exclusivity, and thematic ambition. This contrasts with standard luxury jewelry, which is often more focused on contemporary design and commercial appeal. The report also notes that auction houses highlight not only the physical gemstones but also the stories behind them, including their provenance, rarity, and the cultural or historical context in which they were created [N2-F2].

Overall, sustainability and ethical practice are being integrated into luxury jewelry through material innovation, recycled and lab-grown sourcing, and transparent messaging. The market response is supportive, but the industry remains constrained by price and economic sensitivity, meaning that ethical claims are part of a broader narrative of craftsmanship, heritage, and brand authenticity [N3-R2][N3-R3][N3-R4][N5-F4][N6-R2][N6-R4].
